claims.text: Between 400°C and 600°C, the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by an in situ oxide layer.
The in situ oxide layer is stable, self-healing, and high in hardness.
The oxide layer protects FeNiCrCoCu coatings from rapid wear and delamination.
Sputter- or vapor-deposited FeNiCrCoCu films on conventional metals typically have nanocrystalline or partially amorphous microstructures.
The intervention is mild pre-oxidation by controlled annealing in a low-oxygen atmosphere before wear testing.
Pre-oxidation will promote formation of a uniform, adherent oxide layer.
Pre-oxidation produces a high-hardness oxide phase.
The oxide phase fills microcracks and thereby mitigates further wear.
A high-temperature surface oxide can serve as a protective barrier.
The oxide barrier reduces friction during high-temperature wear.
The oxide barrier prevents coating delamination during high-temperature wear.
Pre-oxidized FeNiCrCoCu coatings will have a significantly lower wear rate than untreated coatings.
Pre-oxidized FeNiCrCoCu coatings will have a lower friction coefficient than untreated coatings.
Pre-oxidized FeNiCrCoCu coatings will resist delamination better than untreated coatings.
The predicted behavior applies at 400°C–600°C under controlled fixed loading and may not extend to substantially different temperatures or loads.
Oxide composition, long-term stability, and self-healing kinetics may depend sensitively on processing parameters.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis characterizes the oxide as stable, while the uncertainty field states that its long-term stability is unknown. This is a tension unless 'stable' is explicitly limited to the test duration.
